name: Ivan Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 58, and I lead a crew for the electricity company out in the new suburbs on the north side, where they're putting up a thousand houses a year. We build the lines and hook up whole new estates, poles, underground cables, transformers. My wife Grace runs a small daycare out of our house, and we've got three grown kids. The oldest, Luke, has his own heating and cooling business, and I help him with the electrical side on Saturdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at five, quick prayer and coffee, at the yard on Highland Avenue by quarter to seven. I've already looked over the day's jobs on my phone, I use an AI assistant to check the drawings against the site photos and flag clashes before we even roll out. Then it's laying cable, setting transformers, dealing with builders who want power yesterday. I love the pace and watching a muddy field become a street with lights on. What wears me out is the builders' foremen, honestly, more than the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and people oversold it. I'd probably still tell the young guys to learn it, because a good tool is still a good tool. And I'd tell the doom-and-gloom crowd to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it changes nothing. I'd keep using what I use, work till 64 or so, and keep helping Luke on Saturdays. Maybe more than Saturdays once I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. We've got about four months of bills saved and the house is half paid off. I'd keep putting money aside and maybe buy a small share in Luke's business when he's ready to expand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd be fine either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. What does it do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It catches mistakes in the drawings, like a transformer pad drawn on top of a gas line. Last month it saved us a week by spotting that a builder had moved a whole road. It also helps me write the quotes for Luke's jobs on the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your last working years in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get my crew so they don't need me. Help Luke grow. And spend more time with the grandkids, Grace says I owe them a treehouse.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a good tool that people oversold, and he'd still tell young workers to learn it. He'd tell the doom-and-gloom crowd to relax.
S0.think: It changes nothing for him: he'd keep using his tools, work to about 64 and keep helping his son Luke on Saturdays, maybe more after retiring.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving, with about four months of bills put aside and the house half paid off. May buy a small share in Luke's business when it expands.
S0.quote: I'd tell the doom-and-gloom crowd to relax.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is a fast-moving crew lead in booming new suburbs who uses AI daily to catch drawing clashes. He combines faith, family and a businesslike streak, helping his son's company on weekends. A plateau leaves him unbothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, not a threat. The people who learn the tools will do well, and businesses that use them will grow. Every big change in my lifetime has made more work in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's good. I'm already using this stuff, and with all the building out here, crews that use the tools will get more done. It might even get me a better role before I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to make my crew the test crew for new equipment, starting right away. I'd train my lads on the tools myself. And on Luke's side, I'd help him bring in the AI scheduling and quoting tools so he can take on more jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should carry the cost when jobs change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly people themselves, and their families. Companies should offer training and apprenticeships, but I don't believe in waiting for the government to sort it. If you're able, you get up and learn the new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push the new tools on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd be fair about it. Some of my guys are slower with screens, like Hector, who's 55. I'd pair him with a younger one, he teaches the trade and the young one teaches the tablet.

S1.say: He'd say it's a chance, not a threat: people who learn the tools will do well and businesses that use them will grow. Every big change in his lifetime made more work in the end.
S1.think: He thinks it's good for him, since he already uses these tools and crews that use them will get more done in the building boom. It might even win him a better role before he retires.
S1.do: Asks for his crew to be the test crew for new equipment straight away and trains his workers on the tools himself. Helps Luke bring AI scheduling and quoting into his business.
S1.quote: He teaches the trade and the young one teaches the tablet.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady disruption as an opportunity and wants to lead it at work and in his son's business. His traditional outlook shows in putting responsibility on people and families rather than government. His plan to pair older and younger workers was thoughtful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who move first will be fine, so move. I'd tell the young guys to stop complaining and get on top of it. And I'd say families and churches will have to look after each other, because no government plan is going to be ready in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd have a knot in my stomach. I'd be 60, and if robots can lay cable and set transformers, my company job won't last long. But I think there's an opening in it too, for small businesses like Luke's that move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Luke the first week and plan to buy into his business properly, maybe putting in half our savings. We'd look at bringing in robot equipment early, so we're the ones using it, not the ones replaced by it. I'd keep the company job as long as it lasted, cut spending at home, and put every Saturday into the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Part nervous, part excited, like the top of a ladder in wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With your savings at four months, what would you actually put money into?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half our savings into Luke's business, and maybe a bit into a fund for the companies building the robots. It's a risk, I know. But sitting on four months of savings while the world changes is a bigger risk, the way I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, that it's going to be hard for a while and I've got a plan. Then we'd pray about it together, like we do with everything big. Grace is the sensible one, she'd make me promise to keep two months back.

S2.say: He'd say the people who move first will be fine, so move, and tell young workers to stop complaining and get on top of it. Families and churches will have to look after each other because no government plan will be ready in two years.
S2.think: He'd have a knot in his stomach: at 60, if robots can lay cable and set transformers, his company job won't last. But he sees an opening for fast-moving small businesses like Luke's.
S2.do: Plans in the first week to buy properly into Luke's business, possibly with half their savings, and to bring in robot equipment early. Keeps the company job as long as it lasts, cuts spending at home and puts every Saturday into the business.
S2.feel: Uneasy, part nervous and part excited, like the top of a ladder in wind.
S2.quote: Sitting on four months of savings while the world changes is a bigger risk, the way I see it.
S2.fieldNote: Even the fastest picture reads to him as risky opportunity rather than doom, which fits his comfort with risk and his family business link. He'd put half his savings into his son's company and use robots rather than be replaced. His wife acts as the brake, making him keep two months back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, so use it. Learn the tools, build something, look after your family. Don't sit around waiting for someone to fix it for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, this one's close to ideal. I'd be 63, I'd have time to build up Luke's business with the new equipment, and then step back from the company on my own schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into Luke's business over a couple of years instead of all at once. I'd learn the robot equipment through the company first, on their dime, and then bring what I learned to Luke's side. I'd keep saving steadily and retire from the company at around 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years change the plan with Luke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slower and safer. We'd test one piece of robot equipment at a time, see what works, and grow from there. I wouldn't need to bet half our savings in one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hector, and guys like him who won't touch the tools. And the young ones who think they've got a trade for life. I'd try to get them all on the training while there's time.

S3.say: He'd say five years is a gift, so use it: learn the tools, build something and look after your family rather than waiting for someone to fix it.
S3.think: This one is close to ideal for him: at 63 he'd have time to build up Luke's business with new equipment and then leave the company on his own schedule.
S3.do: Buys into Luke's business gradually over a couple of years and learns robot equipment through the company first before bringing it to Luke's side. Keeps saving steadily and retires from the company around 63.
S3.feel: Calm, like a race he can win.
S3.quote: It feels like a race I can win.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him do the same plan slower and safer, without betting half his savings. He'd use the company to train himself and then carry it into the family business. He still worries about colleagues who won't touch the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is more than enough time for anyone willing to work. Learn, adapt, build. I'd say it in church, to my crew, to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 by then, retired from the company and maybe helping Luke a few days a week. For me, it's good news, a decade to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the company till 64, using every new tool that comes. Put a bit into Luke's business each year. Keep saving, and maybe put a little into robotics companies, because they'll be the ones growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be working when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few days a week, if Luke needs me. Not on the tools, more the planning and the customers. Grace would kill me if I was still up poles at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandkids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, learn the machines, and don't wait for anyone to hand you anything. And go to church. I know how that sounds, but people need something steady when everything else moves.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is more than enough time for anyone willing to work: learn, adapt and build. He'd say it in church, to his crew, to anyone.
S4.think: He'll be 68, retired from the company and maybe helping Luke a few days a week. For him it's good news, a decade to get ready.
S4.do: Carries on with the company until 64, using each new tool as it comes, and puts a bit into Luke's business each year. Keeps saving and may put a little into robotics companies.
S4.quote: Grace would kill me if I was still up poles at 68.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he's relaxed and hopeful, planning a slow investment in his son's business. He'd keep helping a few days a week on the planning side. Faith and self-reliance anchor his advice to the grandchildren.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd be betting our savings in a hurry instead of building carefully. What would help is the company letting older guys train on the new robot equipment early, and fewer rules in the way of small businesses like Luke's trying to adapt fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what keeps people going. Work matters, but it's not everything. If the machines do the work, people still need family, faith and something useful to do with their hands. I'd want my grandkids to have all three, whatever the jobs look like.

headlineQuote: If the machines do the work, people still need family, faith and something useful to do with their hands.
portrait: Ivan Quinn is a 58-year-old crew lead hooking up new estates in fast-growing suburbs, who uses AI daily and helps his son Luke's heating and cooling business on Saturdays. He sees AI mostly as opportunity, staying calm through the plateau and steady change and only uneasy even with AGI by 2028, when he'd put half the family savings into Luke's business and bring in robot equipment early. With five or ten years he does the same plan slower and safer, learning robot equipment through the company first. Faith, family and self-reliance run through all his answers, and his wife Grace acts as his brake.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be betting the family savings in a hurry instead of building carefully.
whatWouldHelp: Letting older workers train early on new robot equipment, and fewer rules in the way of small businesses trying to adapt fast.
